newsitem.title: JAPAN: Russian tanker spill fouls more of Japan's coast.
newsitem.headline: Russian tanker spill fouls more of Japan's coast.

text.p: The battle against one of Japan's worst oil disasters grew more difficult on Thursday as massive new slicks whipped by heavy winds trebled the stretch of coastline affected by the spill.

A 300-km (190-mile) stretch of once-pristine coastline spanning at least four prefectures facing the Sea of Japan around Kyoto was within the band of oil and was expected to grow wider, the Fisheries Agency said.
"It is highly probable that heavy oil released immediately after the accident will expand the area hit by oil slicks," the agency said in a statement.
The area includes some of Japan's most fertile fishing areas as well as small ports and tourist resorts.
Oil had reached the coastline of Hyogo Prefecture by Thursday morning, about 160 km (100 miles) from where the bow of the ruptured tanker Nakhodka washed up on to rocks.
"It's worse than what we expected," said one fisherman cleaning up the shores at Imagoura in Hyogo Prefecture.
"We have to scoop the oil by hand because the slick is like jelly and won't react to neutralising chemicals or absorbing mats," a Hyoyo prefectural official said.
Normally thriving fish markets along the shore of the fishing port town of Mikuni in Fukui Prefecture were either shut or had only frozen or processed seafood on sale, a rare sight in Japan.
The cleanup operation was still mainly relying on manual labour, with local residents continuing to scoop up oil from the shore by hand, while cranes hauled out oil-filled barrels.
The Transport Ministry has dispatched an oil salvage ship towards Wakasa Bay off Kyoto Prefecture to prevent the damage spreading further, maritime officials said.

Japan had accepted an offer of help from the Russian Transport Ministry and was awaiting a concrete explanation of what Moscow was willing to do, but no action had been taken by the Russians yet, a Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.

Authorities still do not know the full extent of the leakage. They initially estimated that 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil leaked from the tanker but on Tuesday said this figure appeared too low.

The Fisheries Agency said coastal shellfish-gathering operations sustained damage and it feared the oil would harm offshore net and bottom fishing for shrimp and crabs. The agency declined to estimate the value of the losses.
The 13,157-tonne Nakhodka was carrying a total of 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil.
Japan's worst oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil were spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata on the Japan Sea.

Wildlife authorities have reported several cases of seagulls and other birds coated with oil from the latest spill but there have been few reports of harm to wildlife other than fish, seaweed and shellfish.
"We have had one or two reports of dead birds at several places along the...affected areas but nothing serious so far," an official of the Maritime Safety Agency said.
But wildlife experts warned that the toll could grow as the oil became more dispersed.
Hugh Parker, London representative of the International Tanker Owners' Pollution Federation Ltd, who arrived in Japan to survey the scene, said the cleanup work was going very well.
"It is more advanced than I thought it would be," he said.
